newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Olivetti shares suspended - watchdog.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Olivetti shares suspended - watchdog.

text.p: Shares in Italian information technology group Olivetti were suspended in Milan on Thursday pending a meeting between company and market officials, bourse watchdog Consob said.

Consob said it had called a meeting to seek more information after former Olivetti director general Renzo Francesconi said he did not agree with some of the company's half-year results released this week or with some decisions made by the board.

The top management of Olivetti, whose chairman Carlo De Benedetti resigned earlier this week, is expected to attend. Industry sources said Olivetti managing director Francesco Caio would also be there.

Francesconi, who resigned on Wednesday a day after De Benedetti, was quoted in newspapers as saying: "You can make make compromises over strategic plans but you really can't do that with figures and the accounts."
Financial newspapers said Francesconi was signalling that the company's mid-year results did not accurately reflect the depth of Olivetti's financial crisis.
The company, which has not broken even since 1990, announced a pre-tax loss for the first six months of 1996 of 440.2 billion lire ($291 million).
Olivetti shares closed around three percent up on Wednesday at 749.4 lire (50 cents) per share after a brief suspension at the start when the shares breached trading limits.
Caio on Wednesday expressed surprise at Francesconi's statements, saying the half year figures were made on a strict accounting base.

"The figures at June 30 1996 have a strict accounting base and contain provisions which reflect in a correct and considered fashion evaluations in relation to strategic business decisions and the restructuring carried out by the company," Caio said.
Olivetti has been at the heart of a power struggle this week between De Benedetti, who built it up from an ailing type-writer producer, and Caio, who took over as managing director in July.

De Benedetti relinquished his grip suddenly late on Tuesday after nearly 20 years with the company, and the share price, which had fallen nine percent in two days, bounced from near to record lows in relief at the news.

Caio, speaking in a telephone conference call with equity analysts late on Wednesday, said Olivetti's loss-making personal computer company, whose future has been a source of intense market talk, would not reach break-even in 1996.
Some 70 percent of the company's stock is in the hands of overseas institutional investors although De Benedetti still controls around 14 percent.

Investors have speculated Olivetti would try to exit from the highly competitive personal computer sector, either selling off or closing down the PC company which made its name in the 1980s but has not turned a profit for several years.
